content: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is effective in preventing Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) in infants and significantly reduces morbidity and mortality among infants and children who are either living with HIV or exposed to it. Additionally, co-trimoxazole provides protection against common bacterial infections, toxoplasmosis, and malaria. Indications for Co-trimoxazole Administration: 1. Infants born to HIV-infected mothers: Co-trimoxazole should be initiated 4–6 weeks after birth or at the first healthcare encounter. It should be continued until HIV infection is definitively excluded and the infant is no longer at risk of acquiring HIV through breastfeeding. 2. HIV-infected children: Co-trimoxazole should be continued even if the child is on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Duration of Co-trimoxazole Use: Adherence to co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be emphasized at initiation and monitored during every healthcare visit. It is unclear whether co-trimoxazole continues to provide protection after immune system restoration. Children with a history of PCP: Co-trimoxazole should be continued indefinitely. Discontinuation of Co-trimoxazole: Severe adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, renal or hepatic insufficiency, or severe hematological toxicity warrant discontinuation. In HIV-exposed but uninfected children, co-trimoxazole can be stopped when: A non-breastfed child under 18 months has a negative virological test. A breastfed child under 18 months has a negative virological test 6 weeks after breastfeeding cessation. A breastfed child over 18 months has a negative HIV serological test 6 weeks after breastfeeding cessation. In HIV-infected children, co-trimoxazole should be continued until the child is 5 years old and on ART with a sustained CD4 percentage >25%. Co-trimoxazole should not be discontinued if the child is not on ART. Recommended Dosages of Co-trimoxazole: Children under 6 months: One pediatric tablet (20 mg trimethoprim/100 mg sulfamethoxazole) or one-quarter of an adult tablet. Children aged 6 months to 5 years: Two pediatric tablets or half an adult tablet (40 mg trimethoprim/200 mg sulfamethoxazole). Children over 5 years: One adult tablet. For children allergic to co-trimoxazole, dapsone is the preferred alternative, given at 2 mg/kg daily starting from 4 weeks of age. Follow-up Requirements: Tolerance and adherence to co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be assessed at all regular clinic visits. Initially, follow-up may be monthly, transitioning to every 3 months if the medication is well-tolerated. Nutritional Support for HIV-Infected Children: Mothers of HIV-infected infants are encouraged to exclusively breastfeed for 6 months and continue breastfeeding up to 1 year. Older children should consume a varied, energy-rich diet to meet their nutritional needs. Nutritional status, including weight and height, should be routinely assessed during scheduled visits. Energy intake may need to be increased by 25–30% if the child experiences weight loss or poor growth. HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition should be managed according to standard guidelines for uninfected children, with additional energy-rich foods provided. Management of HIV-Related Conditions: 1. Tuberculosis (TB): TB should always be considered in HIV-infected children with symptoms such as cough, fever, or weight loss. Active TB should be treated immediately using the same anti-TB drug regimen as for uninfected children. Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) should be given to HIV-infected children exposed to TB but without active disease, at a dose of 10 mg/kg daily for 6 months. 2. Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PCP): PCP should be suspected in HIV-positive infants with severe pneumonia, particularly those under 12 months of age. Treatment involves high-dose co-trimoxazole (8 mg/kg trimethoprim and 40 mg/kg sulfamethoxazole) three times daily for 3 weeks. If severe drug reactions occur, pentamidine may be used as an alternative. Prednisolone (1–2 mg/kg daily for 1 week) may be helpful in cases of severe hypoxia or respiratory distress. 3. Lymphoid Interstitial Pneumonitis (LIP): LIP may present with persistent cough, bilateral parotid swelling, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and finger-clubbing. Treatment includes oral prednisolone (1–2 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks), with a gradual dose reduction over 2–4 weeks. 4. Fungal Infections: Oral thrush should be treated with nystatin suspension or, if unavailable, gentian violet or miconazole gel. Esophageal candidiasis may require fluconazole (3–6 mg/kg daily for 7 days). 5. Cryptococcal Meningitis: Suspect cryptococcal meningitis in HIV-infected children with signs of meningitis. Diagnosis is confirmed by India ink staining of cerebrospinal fluid. Treatment includes amphotericin B (1 mg/kg daily for 14 days) followed by fluconazole (6–12 mg/kg daily for 8 weeks). 6. Kaposi Sarcoma: Suspect Kaposi sarcoma in children with nodular skin lesions, diffuse lymphadenopathy, or lesions on the palate and conjunctiva. Diagnosis can be confirmed by needle biopsy. Prevention of Mother-to-Child HIV Transmission: HIV-infected pregnant women should receive lifelong ART to improve their health and prevent transmission to their infants during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months, with continued breastfeeding up to 12 months while on ART. Discharge and Referral: HIV-infected children who respond slowly to treatment but are in good general condition can be managed as outpatients. Referral to specialized centers may be necessary for further investigations, second-line treatment, or HIV testing with appropriate counseling.
